title: Single handle every task
hook: 1 restart looks harmless, but what if it is the task tax you keep paying twice?
counterintuition: Why does a day full of work still end with the A-1 task untouched? The costly part may not be the hard task; it may be leaving and coming back again.
tryThisNow: Use tomorrow's first coffee at your usual seat as the event. Count four slow breaths, then pre-write the sentence: "I will finish my A-1 task before I open lower-value work."
keyTakeaway: Choose the A-1 task, start it first, and stay with it until it is done or parked at a clear stopping point.

breakdown.fastRead:
Marc has the A-1 folder open when a smaller message pings. His hand moves toward it, then stops. "If I answer that first, I will have to restart this report," he says. He keeps the folder open and writes the next line.

Single handling means you choose the most important task, begin, and stay with it until it is finished or at a clear stopping point. Completion proves priority. A ranked list only matters when the A-1 task survives the first tempting interruption.
breakdown.deepRead:
Restart costs hide inside switches. When Elaine leaves a hard file for a quick update, she does not return to the same place. She has to reopen the file, find the sentence, remember the aim, and talk herself back into the work.

"It was only two minutes," she tells Nicole in the stockroom doorway.

"Then why are you reading the same page again?" Nicole asks.

That is the cost. Switching makes one task ask for a new start again and again. Each return needs fresh context. Each restart gives resistance another chance to speak. The work may be the same, but the starting line keeps moving.

Single handling protects momentum by making the next behavior plain. Pick the A-1 task. Start immediately. Work without diversion. Finish or reach the defined stop. Those four steps turn priority from a list mark into a visible result.

This does not mean you never pause. If the task is too large for one sitting, name the stopping point before you leave it. Kira writes, "Draft sent to Jacqueline for price check," then closes the file. That is different from drifting away because an easier item waved from the corner.

The final frog habit is simple and stern. Do not let lower-value work vote while the A-1 file is open. Finish the frog before feeding small tasks.
breakdown.fullRead:
Adele is training new hires in the school gym when Jacques raises his hand. "What if the A-1 task takes all day?" he asks. "Do we ignore everything else until midnight?" The group laughs because the question sounds honest.

Single handling breaks when it turns into stubbornness. A hospital call, a safety issue, or a customer waiting on a hard deadline can outrank the task you chose earlier. The rule is not "never stop." The rule is "do not stop for low-value escape."

A defined stopping point keeps the rule sane. If Kira cannot finish the whole budget before the meeting, she writes the exact state of the work: draft complete, two numbers missing, next move is price check. The stop is visible. Anyone can see where to restart.

That matters because vague stopping points are disguised switches. "I will get back to this" asks your future self to rebuild the whole map. "Section two drafted; call Jacqueline for shipping number" leaves a handle on the task. The work waits in one piece instead of scattering across memory.

Lower-value work is sneakier than real interruption. It often arrives wearing a useful badge. A quick inbox sweep looks responsible. A neat file name looks tidy. A small errand looks efficient. But if the frog is still open, those jobs can become a soft exit from the task that matters.

The source idea is completion discipline. In plain words, it means you prove your priority by finishing the thing you ranked first. The proof is not stress, hours, or a busy screen. The proof is a completed task, or a clear stop that protects the next start.

Resistance often drops after sustained work begins. Marc notices this on the third paragraph of the report. The first lines feel heavy. Then the sentence path appears. The smaller message still exists, but it no longer feels urgent enough to steal the report.

This is where the earlier habits join. Clarity names the frog. Priority marks it A-1. Preparation gets the desk ready. Focus keeps lower-value work outside the door. Discipline carries the task to done.

The rule fails when the chosen task is no longer the right task. If Nicole learns that a deadline moved, or Adele gets a true emergency call from the training office, single handling should yield to the new fact. Completion discipline serves results. It should never become a reason to ignore reality.

For ordinary work, though, the test is blunt. Did you start the A-1 task first? Did you stay long enough for resistance to drop? Did you finish, or leave a written handle for the next start? Finished work beats repeated starting.

examples.title: Marc's Open Folder

planSpec.domain: A-1 report threatened by quick messages
planSpec.audience: Marc, an analyst who catches his own switch mid-reach
planSpec.stakes: The ranking method will become decoration if the A-1 task loses to a smaller item.
planSpec.requiredBeat: The protagonist notices his own error mid-stream and corrects course before the A-1 task is abandoned.

examples.scenario: Marc has the A-1 task open, with the source folder under his left hand and a quick message blinking on the monitor. His fingers move to the message before he hears himself say, "I am leaving the frog again." The mistake is the live moment: he sees execution becoming list decoration, not a behavioral commitment. He turns back to the report and works until done.
examples.whatToDo: Marc names the switch out loud, keeps the A-1 folder open, and writes the next paragraph before touching the message.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery shows priority at the moment it is tested. A ranking mark only helps when it changes the next visible act.

examples.title: Elaine's Restart Memo

planSpec.domain: memo about repeated restarts on one client file
planSpec.audience: Elaine, a project lead documenting the cost of switching
planSpec.stakes: Short switches look harmless until the memo shows the same task being restarted several times.
planSpec.requiredBeat: A written artifact carries the action and shows the restart cost inside the document.

examples.scenario: At the stockroom table after the Monday handoff, Elaine sends a project lead memo titled "Client File Restart Log." It reads: "Opened file, checked inbox, reopened file, found page again. Answered Nicole, reopened file, rebuilt price context." Her final line decides the rule: "No more quick switches while the A-1 file is open. Each return makes me pay for the same start twice."
examples.whatToDo: Elaine writes the restart log, names the repeated context rebuild, and protects the open A-1 file from quick switches.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo makes restart cost visible. Once the reader can see the repeated reopening, switching no longer looks free.

examples.title: Jacqueline and Nicole Finish Differently

planSpec.domain: two teammates handling the same final frog habit
planSpec.audience: Jacqueline and Nicole, teammates with opposite responses to one priority
planSpec.stakes: One person can look busy while the other proves priority through completion.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Two named people approach the same situation in opposite ways and the outcomes diverge.

examples.scenario: Before lunch at the shared worktable, Jacqueline clears six small tickets and says the morning was productive. The A-1 proposal still has a blank recommendation. Nicole, the reviewer, ignores the small tickets. She drafts the recommendation and marks the proposal ready. Jacqueline has activity to report. Nicole has the frog moved to a finished state.
examples.whatToDo: Nicole keeps the final frog habit tied to the recommendation paragraph and finishes that piece before touching the small tickets.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast separates motion from completion. The reader learns to ask what finished, not how busy the morning looked.

examples.title: Adele Hears the Cost

planSpec.domain: peer coaching after repeated context loss
planSpec.audience: Adele, a coordinator stuck in restart fatigue
planSpec.stakes: She reads tiredness as a reason to switch when switching is making the work heavier.
planSpec.requiredBeat: A peer reframes the stuck view in one conversation with a quotable sentence.

examples.scenario: "I am tired of this file," Adele says on the phone. Kira asks how many times she has rebuilt context and reopened materials today. "Four." Kira answers, "You are not tired from working; you are tired from restarting." Adele hears the resistance in the switches, then reads the next paragraph aloud so she can stay with the file.
examples.whatToDo: Adele accepts the reframe, reads the next paragraph aloud, and stays with the file until the marked section is complete.
examples.whyItMatters: The talk changes the cause she sees. If restart cost is the fatigue, another switch will not give the reader relief.

examples.title: Jacques Ranks Before Starting

planSpec.domain: training session on choosing before single handling
planSpec.audience: Jacques, a learner who confuses staying busy with choosing the A-1 task
planSpec.stakes: Single handling cannot work if the learner never chooses the true priority first.
planSpec.requiredBeat: A learning context uses the learner's confusion as the material.

examples.scenario: In the school gym training, Jacques circles three tasks and asks, "Which one do I single handle?" Adele points to the blank A-1 column on his execution sheet. "First rank them. Single handling needs the A-1 task until done." Jacques frowns, then treats the mark as a behavioral commitment and crosses out the lower-value warm-up email.
examples.whatToDo: Jacques ranks the list first, marks the grant draft A-1, and starts that task instead of the easier email.
examples.whyItMatters: The confusion is useful because it exposes the precondition. Single handling begins after priority is named, not before.

examples.title: Kira Leaves a Handle

planSpec.domain: budget draft stopped once with fog and once with a written handle
planSpec.audience: Kira, a peer coach showing her own before and after
planSpec.stakes: Stopping without a clear handle makes the next start carry the whole restart cost.
planSpec.requiredBeat: The same person is shown earlier and later with one variable changed: a defined stopping point.

examples.scenario: Last week, Kira shut the budget draft with only "finish later" in the margin. The restart was slow: she reopened materials, rebuilt context, and felt resistance rise. This week, at the coffee table, she writes, "Draft complete through travel; next is vendor price check." The task is not finished. The stopping point is defined, and the next start has a handle.
examples.whatToDo: Kira writes the exact stopping point and the next move before closing the budget draft.
examples.whyItMatters: A defined stop is not failure. It protects the next start when full completion is not possible yet.

questions.prompt: Marc and Elaine both open an A-1 report. Marc stays with the open file; Elaine answers every small request as it appears. Which response matches single handling?
choices: Elaine matches it because each request gets handled while it is fresh.
Elaine matches it because no one task should hold the whole work block.
Marc matches it because the chosen task stays active until completion.
questions.explanation: Single handling keeps the chosen task active until completion. The request-by-request answer treats interruption as equal to progress.

questions.prompt: Jacques has three marked tasks on his training sheet: grant draft A-1, inbox cleanup B-2, and receipt sorting C-1. Where should his first work block begin?
choices: The grant draft should begin the block because it carries the A-1 mark.
The inbox cleanup should begin the block because it is already visible.
The receipt sorting should begin the block because it can be cleared fast.
questions.explanation: The A-1 task starts first. The visible and quick tasks are plausible near misses, but they let ease outrank priority.

questions.prompt: Elaine's restart log shows one client file opened five times, with email checks between each return. Which reading fits the warning about switching?
choices: The email checks refreshed attention by changing the work often.
The repeated returns raised the cost by making context rebuild.
The five openings showed the file needed more research before drafting.
questions.explanation: The log points to restart cost: each return asks Elaine to rebuild context. The energy and research readings miss the repeated restarting.

questions.prompt: Jacqueline clears eight tiny tickets while Nicole finishes the proposal recommendation. Which result carries more weight in completion discipline?
choices: Nicole's finished recommendation carries more weight than Jacqueline's activity count.
Jacqueline's eight tickets carry more weight because the count is higher.
Both results carry equal weight because both workers stayed visibly busy.
questions.explanation: Completion matters more than activity. Jacqueline's count can look strong while the main frog remains unfinished.

questions.prompt: During Adele's call, the A-1 file is open and the next paragraph is marked. A three-minute inbox sweep appears before she finishes. What should happen next?
choices: Adele should finish the marked section before opening the inbox sweep.
Adele should clear the inbox sweep because three minutes is a small cost.
Adele should switch to the inbox sweep if it makes the desk feel lighter.
questions.explanation: Lower-value work should not interrupt the frog. The inbox sweep looks harmless because it is short, but it still pulls Adele away.

questions.prompt: Marc and Kira both feel resistance before a hard page. Marc waits for the feeling to fade; Kira works through the first page. Which pattern does the source fact support?
choices: Marc's wait fits because resistance usually rises during focused work.
Kira's first page fits because resistance often drops after sustained work.
Marc's wait fits when easier tasks can build a better mood first.
questions.explanation: Resistance often drops after sustained work begins. Waiting for the feeling to disappear puts comfort before action.

questions.prompt: Kira cannot finish the whole budget before the meeting, but she can leave one note on the draft. Which note protects the next start?
choices: I will finish this later when I have a better block.
The budget is still open, so this stop does not count.
Draft complete through travel; next is vendor price check.
questions.explanation: A defined stopping point is acceptable when full completion is impossible. Kira's specific note shows what is done and what comes next.

questions.prompt: Jacques asks Adele which of three useful tasks deserves single handling, but the list has no rank marks. What has to come before the start?
choices: He should choose the task that feels easiest to finish.
He should work on all three until one choice becomes obvious.
He should rank the list so the A-1 task is named first.
questions.explanation: Single handling requires prior prioritization. Without the A-1 mark, Jacques is just choosing by feel or activity.

questions.prompt: Adele's closing checklist puts clarity, priority, focus, and discipline beside one daily behavior. Which behavior completes that set?
choices: Preparing several possible tasks so the day stays flexible.
Choosing the A-1 task, starting it, and carrying it to done.
Moving among several tasks so each habit gets equal attention.
questions.explanation: The final habit joins earlier methods into one behavior: choose the A-1 task, start it, and carry it to done.

reviewCards.front: What does completion discipline ask you to do after you choose the A-1 task?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to begin the A-1 task and stay with it until it is finished or left at a clear stopping point.

reviewCards.front: Why do small switches make one hard task cost more?
reviewCards.back: Each switch makes you rebuild context, reopen materials, and face resistance again. The task is the same, but the start repeats.

reviewCards.front: How does the final frog habit turn daily discipline into progress?
reviewCards.back: It asks whether you finish the frog before lower-value work gets a vote. Daily discipline means A-1 moves, not just that many small tasks got attention.

reviewCards.front: When is it acceptable to stop before the whole task is finished?
reviewCards.back: Stop when full completion is not possible and the stopping point is written clearly. The note must show what is done and what comes next.

reviewCards.front: In one sentence, how does frictionless start (Ch 9) connect to completion discipline?
reviewCards.back: A frictionless start clears the desk for one task; completion discipline keeps that chosen task protected until it is finished.

reviewCards.front: What is the danger of quick lower-value work while the frog is open?
reviewCards.back: It feels useful, but it can become a soft exit from the task that matters. Quick work should wait while the A-1 task is active.

implementationPlan.title: Prewrite the Finish Line
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice protecting the A-1 task with words you have already written. Prewrite the Finish Line by naming the task, the lower-value work you will delay, and the sentence you will say when a switch tempts you. The skill is simple: start first, stay longer, and leave a clear handle if you must stop.

ifThenPlans.context: The work block begins and several tasks look useful.
ifThenPlans.plan: If several tasks call for attention, then read the A-1 line first and begin that task before opening lower-value work.
If a quick switch tempts you, then count four slow breaths and say the prewritten line that keeps you with the open task.

ifThenPlans.context: Full completion is not possible yet.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you must stop, then write what is done and the exact next move before closing the file.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, during your first coffee or first commute pause, pre-write the words you will use when a quick task interrupts your A-1 work. Count four slow breaths before writing the line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, tally each time lower-value work interrupts an open A-1 task. At week's end, read the number and pre-write one stronger refusal line.

memorableLines.why: It gives the chapter's core test in three words.
It makes the invisible price of task switching memorable.
It closes the chapter with a portable behavior test.
